content: Without proper utilization, a product may not achieve its full potential, leading to financial losses and potentially compromising user safety. 3D Printing in Prosthetics and Orthotics For decades, computer-aided design and manufacturing techniques have been employed in prosthetics and orthotics to create shape-captured models of body segments. However, the advent of 3D printing has introduced significant advancements in traditional fabrication methods. Over the past 20 years, additive manufacturing, which involves layering materials (commonly thermoplastics), has been applied to this field. This method eliminates the need for plaster casts or molds, making it a cleaner and less invasive process, particularly beneficial for children. Additionally, it reduces production time for devices. The 3D printing process typically begins with a 3D scanner capturing the dimensions of the body segment. Images from various angles are digitally combined to create a 3D image file, which is then sent to a 3D printer. This technology allows for the creation of custom devices or specific component parts. Advances in materials and technology have made prosthetic sockets, orthoses, and components durable enough to meet ISO testing standards and withstand daily use. Furthermore, 3D printers are now capable of producing full-length prostheses and orthoses, and the cost of scanners and printers is decreasing as demand grows. However, 3D printing is not a universal solution. Clinicians in prosthetics and orthotics must understand the advantages and limitations of 3D printing compared to conventional methods. With proper training and the strengthening of core service components, 3D printing and other technological advancements can enhance access to prostheses and orthoses for the majority of individuals who currently lack access. These innovations also improve user choice and experience in existing services. Prefabricated and Custom-Made Products Prosthetics and orthotics service providers often use both prefabricated and custom-made products. Both types require fitting and adjustment to match the user’s anatomical features. The choice of product should be guided by an evaluation of its potential to achieve a good fit, comfort, functionality, safety, quality, and cost. Economic factors in the service environment also influence this decision. These products are often designed for temporary or single use and are readily available in hospital units and primary healthcare services. While prefabricated products may allow for faster fitting and lower costs, they may be less effective and should only be used when satisfactory results can be achieved. In low-income settings, the cost of storing prefabricated products may be prohibitive, making individual fabrication more cost-effective. Custom-made products, including upperand lower-limb prostheses and orthoses, are typically chosen when a closer fit, better functionality, or stronger support is required. These products are constructed from a variety of materials, such as plastics, metals, leather, carbon fiber, and composite materials, and may incorporate prefabricated components tailored to the user’s needs. Priority Assistive Products The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that over one billion people require one or more assistive products for mobility, vision, hearing, communication, or cognition. To improve access to high-quality, affordable assistive products globally, WHO’s Global Cooperation on Assistive Technology (GATE) initiative developed a priority assistive products list. This list, created in consultation with experts, users, and caregivers, identifies 50 essential products, including prosthetic and orthotic devices, that are critical for maintaining or improving individual functioning. These products should be available at prices affordable to communities or countries. It also raises public awareness, mobilizes resources, guides product development, and stimulates competition, thereby increasing global access to assistive products. Governments can use this model to define national priorities for prosthetics, orthotics, and mobility products, contributing to universal health coverage and the development of reimbursement policies, including insurance coverage. ISO standards cover various industries, including healthcare and assistive products. For prosthetics and orthotics, specific ISO standards (e.g., ISO 8549 and ISO 13405) provide methods and terminology for product categorization and description. These standards should be used for national classification of prosthetic and orthotic products. Supply of Components and Materials Efficient procurement and logistics are essential for cost-effective and uninterrupted prosthetics and orthotics services. In larger organizations, procurement may be handled by a dedicated office, while smaller units may delegate this responsibility to regular staff. While basic materials like plastics, plaster of Paris, wood, and leather are widely available, certain components must be imported. Importation can be challenging, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, due to lengthy and costly customs clearance processes. National stakeholders should collaborate with authorities to exempt prosthetic and orthotic materials from import taxes and simplify importation procedures. Centralized procurement offices and stores can facilitate the distribution of components and materials, reduce costs, and streamline importation processes. Computer software can aid in managing stock, recording values, preparing purchase orders, and calculating service costs. In larger service units, stock management should be assigned to a dedicated storekeeper, and storage areas should be separate from workshop spaces. Reuse and Donation of Components Reusing prosthetic and orthotic components can reduce costs and assist more individuals. Used products should be refurbished under controlled conditions, decontaminated, and approved before reuse. Users must be informed when reused components are integrated into their devices. Customized parts, such as prosthetic sockets, should never be reused. Donations of used prostheses and orthoses from high-income countries to lowand middle-income countries, while well-intentioned, are not always beneficial. Custom-made devices are unlikely to fit new users, and donated components may not be compatible with local technology. Waste Management Prosthetics and orthotics services generate waste, some of which may harm the environment. Proper disposal of waste materials, including hazardous products, is essential. Users should return unused devices to service providers for disassembly, reuse of components, and appropriate disposal of remaining materials. Regulations should cover product supply, material importation, and component reuse, adhering to ISO standards where applicable. Structural and Clinical Testing Prosthetic and orthotic components must be durable to prevent device failure and user injury. Structural and clinical field tests should assess the strength, durability, lifespan, and biocompatibility of components. Structural testing follows ISO specifications, while clinical testing evaluates functionality, safety, and effectiveness in real-world conditions. Testing should adhere to ethical regulations, with informed consent from participants. Research and Development Research is vital for advancing prosthetics and orthotics services. However, most research benefits high-income countries, with limited attention to the needs of lowand middle-income countries. WHO has identified five priority research areas, including the effects and costs of assistive technology, policies and service delivery models, and the development of affordable, high-quality products. National centers of excellence should coordinate research initiatives and support training in research for relevant personnel. Development of Affordable Products Prosthetic and orthotic components are produced globally, but most research and development focus on high-income markets. There is a need for affordable designs that reduce costs and increase access in lowand middle-income countries. Mass production of cost-effective, high-quality components could address global needs and create new business opportunities. Achieving this goal requires collaboration among national and international stakeholders, including experts, entrepreneurs, governments, and funding agencies.
